usage: Said when someone freezes up or gets caught off guard; 하지 마 is the standard casual 'don't'.
I was so caught off guard
-잖아 invites shared understanding: 'you know I was flustered, right?'
Could you tell I was flustered?
티(가) 나다 = '(a feeling) shows'; 당황한 티 = the flustered look that leaks out.
You springing that on me is bewildering
당황스럽다 (adjective) describes the SITUATION as awkward/bewildering, vs 당황하다 the felt reaction.
examples: 갑자기 영어로 물어봐서 완전 당황했어.
They suddenly asked me in English so I totally froze.
완전 ('totally') is the everyday intensifier here; 갑자기 = 'all of a sudden'.
카드가 안 돼서 계산대에서 당황했어.
My card got declined and I panicked at the checkout.
계산대 = the cashier/checkout counter; ~아서/어서 links cause ('because X, I got flustered').
이름을 잘못 불러서 완전 당황했어.
I totally panicked because I called the wrong name.
~아서/어서 당황하다 = panic because of something; everyday slip-up situation.
nuance: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard — the perfect word for a 'my brain went blank' instant, NOT prolonged panic or dread. The Sino-Korean root is 唐慌: 唐 'abrupt/sudden' + 慌 'flurried, panicked', so it literally paints a sudden flurry of mind. Compare its neighbors: 긴장하다 (緊張) is the nervous tension you feel BEFORE an event (a held breath), while 당황하다 is the scramble in the MOMENT something unexpected hits. 놀라다 is plain 'be startled/surprised'; 당황하다 adds the 'and now I don't know what to do' confusion on top. The big English-speaker pitfall: don't say 당황돼 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 already encodes the felt experience and is not normally built with 되다, so use 당황해 / 당황했어. Also keep the adjective 당황스럽다 ('the situation is bewildering') separate from the verb 당황하다 ('I got flustered').

usage: Teasing a partner or friend; playful tone is common.
For envy-without-resentment ('lucky you!'), Koreans say 부럽다, NOT 질투하다.
질투(가) 나다 ('jealousy arises') is the natural way to report the feeling, vs the heavier 질투해.
질투심 (嫉妬心) = 'the feeling of jealousy'; 때문에 = 'because of', names the inner cause.
examples: 남친이 여사친 많아서 좀 질투해.
My boyfriend has a lot of female friends so I get a bit jealous.
남친 = 남자친구 (boyfriend), 여사친 = 여자 사람 친구 (female friend) — essential dating slang.
친구가 나보다 잘돼서 질투하는 내가 너무 싫어.
I hate that I'm jealous of my friend doing better than me.
잘되다 = 'to go well / succeed'; 나보다 = 'than me'. Honest self-talk.
걔 인스타 보면 가끔 질투 나.
When I see their Instagram I sometimes get jealous.
질투(가) 나다 is more natural than 질투하다 for a passing twinge; 걔 = 'that person (casual)'.
nuance: 질투하다 carries a sharp, possessive jealousy — the romantic or competitive sting of 'they have what I want and it bothers me'. The hanja is 嫉妬, where BOTH characters (嫉 and 妬) literally mean envy/jealousy, doubling the intensity. The crucial dividing line for English speakers: English 'jealous' is used loosely for mild envy, but Korean splits it. 부럽다 = harmless, friendly envy ('lucky you, I wish I had that') and is what you say ~90% of the time; saying 부러워 warms a conversation. 질투하다 / 질투 나다 is the bitter, edged version, and accusing a friend of 질투해 can genuinely sting. Also note register: to report the feeling, 질투(가) 나 ('I feel jealous') sounds more natural and less self-incriminating than the bald 질투해. Pitfall: never reach for 질투하다 when you just mean 'how nice for you' — that is 부럽다, full stop.

usage: The standard motivational line — friends, coaches, dramas all use it.
-(으)ㄹ래 expresses your own decision/intention; resigned tone.
to give up on a dream
Takes object + 을/를: 꿈을 / 목표를 / 시험을 포기하다 — abandon a concrete goal.
It'd be too much of a waste to quit
~기엔 너무 아깝다 = 'to (do) is too regrettable'; the classic anti-giving-up phrase.
examples: 다이어트는 진작에 포기했어.
I gave up on the diet ages ago.
진작에 = 'long ago / already'; 다이어트 포기 is a relatable running joke.
집값 보고 서울에 집 사는 건 포기했어.
After seeing the prices, I gave up on buying a place in Seoul.
집값 = housing prices; ~는 건 포기하다 = 'give up on doing'. A very real 20-30s concern.
여기까지 왔는데 지금 포기하기엔 너무 아까워.
We've come this far — it'd be a waste to give up now.
아깝다 = 'too good to waste'; 여기까지 왔는데 = 'having come this far'.
nuance: 포기하다 = to give up, abandon, or relinquish a goal, plan, claim, or even a person. The hanja 抛棄 is vivid: 抛 'to throw/hurl away' + 棄 'to discard, abandon', so the image is hurling something aside and walking off — a decisive letting-go, not a gentle fade. Contrast 포기하다 (stop pursuing a goal entirely) with 그만두다 (stop/quit an ongoing activity — a job, a habit) and with 단념하다 (a more bookish 'resign oneself to abandoning hope'); in speech 포기하다 is the everyday choice. Grammar: it pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or with 는 거 / 는 걸 (사는 걸 포기하다 = 'give up on buying'). Culturally the word is loaded: N포세대, the 'give-up generation', names young Koreans said to have surrendered dating, marriage, and kids to economic pressure. English-speaker pitfall: the negative is 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), NOT 안 포기해.

usage: Encouraging someone to try something new/bold; 한번 = 'just once, give it a go'.
I love taking on new things
도전하다 takes 에 for the target of the challenge.
도전 정신 (挑戰精神) = the admired 'spirit of taking things on'; common in self-intros and résumés.
This time I'll definitely give it a go
도전해 보다 = 'try taking it on'; 꼭 = 'for sure', a determined promise to yourself.
examples: 올해는 마라톤에 도전해 보려고.
This year I'm going to try taking on a marathon.
~에 도전하다; ~(으)려고 = 'I intend/plan to'. Common New Year goal talk.
새로운 분야에 도전하고 싶어서 이직했어.
I changed jobs because I wanted to take on a new field.
이직하다 = 'to change jobs', big in 20-30s career talk; 분야 = field/area.
매운 거 잘 못 먹는데 불닭볶음면 한번 도전해 볼게.
I'm bad with spicy food but I'll give fire-noodles a try.
불닭볶음면 = the famous super-spicy instant noodle; 도전해 볼게 = 'I'll give it a try'.
nuance: 도전하다 = to take something on, rise to a challenge, brave a new or daunting endeavor — overwhelmingly positive and aspirational (a job change, a new hobby, scary spicy food, a hard exam). The hanja 挑戰 literally means 挑 'provoke, stir up' + 戰 'battle', i.e. 'to pick a fight', and that combative root explains both senses: figuratively you 'do battle' with a goal. Particle pitfall for English speakers: it takes 에, not 을/를 — 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), 시험에 도전하다. Contrast it with 노력하다 (sustained, grinding effort over time) and 시도하다 (a neutral, often one-off 'attempt'): 도전하다 specifically frames the target as bold or intimidating, with a brave-the-unknown flavor. Note: it does NOT mean confronting a person in an argument — 'to challenge someone' in that sense is 이의를 제기하다 or 도전장을 내밀다, not plain 도전하다. The everyday encouragement is 도전해 봐.

usage: Sincere promise to put in effort; softer and warmer than a firm guarantee.
-는 중이야 = 'in the middle of'; common honest reply.
잘하려고 노력해 = 'I try to do well'; the standard frame for 'try to + verb' as sustained effort.
보람이 있다 = '(the effort) was worthwhile'; the satisfying counterpart to wasted effort.
examples: 한국어 늘리려고 매일 노력하고 있어.
I'm making an effort every day to improve my Korean.
늘리다 ('to improve/build up'); ~(으)려고 expresses purpose. Perfect learner sentence.
노력한 만큼 결과가 안 나와서 속상해.
The results don't match my effort, and it's upsetting.
~한 만큼 = 'as much as (I) did'; 속상하다 = 'to be upset/heartsick'.
관계는 한 사람만 노력하면 안 돼.
A relationship can't work if only one person tries.
관계 = relationship; ~만 ...면 안 돼 = 'it won't do if only...'. Relatable dating wisdom.
nuance: 노력하다 = to make an effort, try hard, put sustained work toward a goal. The hanja 努力 spells out the meaning: 努 'to exert oneself, strain' + 力 'strength/power' — literally 'to exert one's strength', a grind-it-out word. Distinguish three look-alikes English flattens into 'try': 노력하다 = ongoing, earnest effort over time; 도전하다 = boldly taking on a fresh challenge; 시도하다 = a neutral one-off attempt. So 'I'll try harder' is 더 노력할게, never 더 도전할게. Its signature frame is ~(으)려고 노력하다 = 'try to (do)', as in 일찍 일어나려고 노력해. Culturally, effort itself is praised in Korea — 노력파 ('the hardworking type') is a compliment, and 노력할게 is a warm, sincere thing to promise. English-speaker pitfall: 노력하다 means putting in effort, not merely 'attempting once'; for 'let me try this button', that's 한번 해 볼게, not 노력할게.

usage: Just hold on a little longer
Gritty encouragement — survive the hard part; 조금만 더 = 'just a bit more'.
I have to hold out till payday
Very real 20s money humor; 월급날 = payday, ~까지 버티다 = 'hold out until'.
커피로 버티다 / 라면으로 버티다 = scrape through on coffee / instant noodles.
to tough it out to the end
끝까지 = 'all the way to the end'; pairs naturally with 포기하지 말고 버텨.
examples: 커피로 버티면서 시험 기간 넘겼어.
I got through exam season running on coffee.
~(으)로 버티다 = 'get by on'; 시험 기간 = exam period. Universal student life.
상사가 진상이라 1년 버티고 퇴사했어.
My boss was awful so I held out a year and then quit.
진상 = a nasty/awful person (slang); 퇴사하다 = 'to quit one's job'.
여기서 포기하지 말고 끝까지 버텨 보자.
Don't give up here — let's tough it out to the end.
끝까지 = 'to the very end'; pairs naturally with 포기하지 말다 in one breath.
nuance: 버티다 = to hold out, hang on, withstand, or scrape through a hard stretch — often financially or under pressure (a brutal job, no money, exam season). It is a pure native Korean verb (no hanja), and that street-level texture matters: 버티다 is grittier and more colloquial than its near-synonym 견디다. The line between them: 견디다 leans toward passively 'enduring/bearing' pain or hardship, while 버티다 adds an active 'dig-in-your-heels and refuse to collapse' stance — holding a position against a force. So young Koreans joke 월급날까지 버틴다 ('surviving till payday') and 일단 버텨 ('just hang in there for now'). Conjugation note: it's a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 버티 + 어 contracts to 버텨, and the past is 버티 + 었어 → 버텼어 (one syllable, not 버티었어). Pitfall: don't write the past as 버티었어 or 버텼써 — the correct spelling is 버텼어.

usage: ~아/어 줘서 고마워 = 'thanks for (doing) for me'; very common.
위로가 되다 = 'to be a comfort'; natural reply when someone's words helped.
위로 as a noun + 받다 ('receive'); the receiving side of 위로해 주다.
위로의 말(을) 건네다 = 'offer words of comfort'; set phrase for condolences and support.
examples: 친구가 힘들 때 옆에서 위로해 줬어.
My friend comforted me when I was going through a hard time.
옆에서 ('by my side') + 위로해 주다 — the benefactive 주다 is almost always attached.
말없이 안아주는 게 제일 큰 위로였어.
Just being hugged without words was the biggest comfort.
위로 as a noun ('comfort'); 말없이 = 'without words', 안아주다 = 'to hug (someone)'.
장례식에서 유가족을 어떻게 위로해야 할지 몰라서 그냥 손을 잡아 드렸어.
At the funeral I didn't know how to comfort the bereaved family, so I just held their hand.
유가족 = the bereaved family; ~해야 할지 몰라서 = 'not knowing how I should'. A weighty real moment.
nuance: 위로하다 = to comfort or console someone in pain, grief, or loss. The hanja 慰勞 is telling: 慰 'to soothe, console' + 勞 'toil, weariness', i.e. to soothe another's hardship — so the word carries real emotional weight and suits sorrow, bereavement, and exhaustion, not light cheering-up. In practice it almost always appears as 위로해 주다 (with the benefactive 주다, because comfort is something you GIVE someone) or as the noun 위로 (위로가 되다 'to be a comfort', 위로를 받다 'to be comforted'). Contrast it sharply with 응원하다: you 위로해 someone who is hurting or grieving, but you 응원해 someone facing a challenge ahead — comfort looks back at pain, cheering looks forward to a goal. The big English-speaker pitfall: dropping 주다. '나는 친구를 위로했어' is grammatical but sounds clinical and detached, like a report; the warm, natural sentence is 친구를 위로해 줬어.

Using 위로하다 to root for someone before a challenge — that's 응원하다; 위로하다 is for someone already hurting or grieving.

usage: I'll always be rooting for you
Warm, supportive send-off; common in messages and goodbyes.
Cheer me on / Wish me luck
Asking for support before a big thing; ~아/어 줘 = 'do it for me'.
응원 메시지 / 응원 댓글 = encouraging message / comment; ubiquitous on social media and to idols/athletes.
I'm cheering you on in my heart
마음으로 = 'in (my) heart'; softens it to quiet, from-afar support.
examples: 새 직장 잘되길 응원할게!
I'm rooting for your new job to go well!
잘되길 (= 잘되기를) 응원하다 = 'cheer for it to go well'; sweet, everyday support.
나 항상 네 편이고 응원해.
I'm always on your side and rooting for you.
네 편이다 = 'to be on your side'; pairs naturally with 응원하다.
손흥민 경기 있어서 친구들이랑 모여서 다 같이 응원했어.
There was a Son Heung-min match so we gathered and all cheered together.
응원하다 also = cheering for a sports team; 모이다 = 'to gather'. Football-watch culture.
nuance: 응원하다 = to cheer on, root for, and actively support — both literally (yelling for a sports team, 응원단 = a cheering squad) and emotionally (backing a friend's goals). The hanja 應援 says it well: 應 'to respond' + 援 'to aid, rescue', i.e. to answer someone's effort with support. The key contrast is with 위로하다: 응원하다 looks FORWARD and is upbeat — you cheer someone on toward a challenge or future ('you've got this!') — whereas 위로하다 looks BACK at pain to console it. So 응원해 / 응원할게 is lighter and brighter than 위로해. It often takes the benefactive 응원해 줘 when you ask others for support. Telling someone 항상 응원할게 ('I'll always be rooting for you') is one of the warmest, most natural send-offs in Korean. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 응원하다 when someone is grieving or hurting — that calls for 위로하다 (comfort), not a pep-talk cheer.

mistakes: Confusing 응원하다 (cheer toward a goal) with 위로하다 (comfort in sadness) — you 응원해 someone facing a challenge, but 위로해 someone who's hurting.
Saying 너를 응원해 to a heartbroken friend in mourning — cheering can feel tone-deaf there; offer 위로 (comfort) instead, e.g. 많이 힘들지... 내가 옆에 있을게.
